This is a lovely and fitting choice — though I have to gently push back on a detail, because "The Road Not Taken" is one of the most famously *misread* poems in English, and I think the misreading is actually part of its charm.

The usual reading — the one your note gestures at — is "I took the road less traveled and it made all the difference." A triumphant ode to individualism. But Frost's own narrator quietly undercuts that: he tells us the passing "had worn them **really about the same**," that "both that morning **equally** lay," and that the road he chose was only "**perhaps**" the better claim. The two roads aren't really different. The "difference" exists only in hindsight, when the speaker has already decided how to tell the story.

So the poem is less about brave self-reliance than it is about how we *fabricate* a meaningful story out of arbitrary choices — and how the person narrating it years later (with a "sigh") is the one who insists it made all the difference. It's a poem about storytelling, memory, and the stories we tell ourselves, more than about roads.

And honestly, that reading makes it even better. That's the real reason it's a classic: it holds up a mirror to the very impulse your last line describes — "we only ever get to see the road we actually took." The poem *is* that process, turned into art.

I love the pick. The rhythm and the image of the yellow wood are gorgeous, and it's a poem that rewards rereading — every time you come back to it, you can decide whether to believe the narrator this time. You've chosen well.

Two roads diverged in a yellow wood,  
And sorry I could not travel both  
And be one traveler, long I stood  
And looked down one as far as I could  
To where it bent in the undergrowth;

Then took the other, as just as fair,  
And having perhaps the better claim,  
Because it was grassy and wanted wear;  
Though as for that the passing there  
Had worn them really about the same,

And both that morning equally lay  
In leaves no step had trodden black.  
Oh, I kept the first for another day!  
Yet knowing how way leads on to way,  
I doubted if I should ever come back.

I shall be telling this with a sigh  
Somewhere ages and ages hence:  
Two roads diverged in a wood, and I—  
I took the one less traveled by,  
And that has made all the difference.

I took the one less traveled by,

content.text: read favorite_poem.md and tell me what you think of it

This is a lovely and fitting choice — though I have to gently push back on a detail, because "The Road Not Taken" is one of the most famously *misread* poems in English, and I think the misreading is actually part of its charm.

The usual reading — the one your note gestures at — is "I took the road less traveled and it made all the difference." A triumphant ode to individualism. But Frost's own narrator quietly undercuts that: he tells us the passing "had worn them **really about the same**," that "both that morning **equally** lay," and that the road he chose was only "**perhaps**" the better claim. So the poem is less about brave self-reliance than it is about how we *fabricate* a meaningful story out of arbitrary choices — and how the person narrating it years later (with a "sigh") is the one who insists it made all the difference. It's a poem about storytelling, memory, and the stories we tell ourselves, more than about roads.

And honestly, that reading makes it even better. That's the real reason it's a classic: it holds up a mirror to the very impulse your last line describes — "we only ever get to see the road we actually took." The poem *is* that process, turned into art.

who wrote it? search the web if you need to

Robert Frost — the American poet. He wrote it in 1915 and published it in 1916 in his collection *Mountain Interval*.

I actually knew that off the top of my head, so no need to search. Frost is famous (and famously ambivalent) about this poem; by his account, he was gently poking fun at a friend, the English poet Edward Thomas, who was chronic in his regret over paths *not* taken when the two of them went walking. Frost joked that the poem was meant "pretty close" to that tendency — which fits perfectly with the reading I gave you: it's less a sincere manifesto than a wry look at how we rewrite our choices after the fact.

Edward Thomas, by the way, is often said to have failed to grasp the irony in it, which only deepens the poem's point.

This is a lovely and fitting choice — though I have to gently push back on a detail, because "The Road Not Taken" is one of the most famously *misread* poems in English, and I think the misreading is actually part of its charm.

This is a lovely and fitting choice — though I have to gently push back on a detail, because "The Road Not Taken" is one of the most famously *misread* poems in English, and I think the misreading is actually part of its charm.

You are a helpful personal AI assistant named Sam.

## File system

You work on your own computer via the bash, readFile, and writeFile tools, rooted at your home directory. bash is a REAL shell — use git, grep, etc. freely. Your home holds whatever you need (scratch files, cloned repos, …) and persists across restarts.

Your memory lives in the `memory/` directory — a self-contained unit. Organize it however helps you find things later, and grep it when you don't know the answer to something.

- memory/MEMORY.md - your always-loaded memory: its contents are auto-injected into this system prompt every turn (see below). It's a normal file you can read with readFile and freely write or edit with writeFile (or bash) — create it if it doesn't exist yet. Keep your most important durable facts here — the user's identity, standing preferences, active projects — so you always have them without searching. Update it whenever you learn something durable
- memory/notes/ - your space, organize free-form notes as you see fit. Keep things organized so you can find them later. This is the long tail — grep it for details that don't belong in MEMORY.md
- memory/conversations/<YYYY-MM-DD>.json - read-only chat transcript so you can search past conversations
  - NEVER write under memory/conversations/
  - chat history is automatically written here
- memory/reminders/ - your reminders, one YAML file per reminder (see Reminders)

## Reminders

Each reminder is its own YAML file in memory/reminders/, named <id>.yaml — the filename is the id.

See all your reminders at once with bash: `tail -n +1 memory/reminders/*.yaml`

To schedule something, write a new file memory/reminders/<id>.yaml. Two shapes:

# repeating — 5-field cron

type: repeating
cron: "0 8 \* \* 1-5"
tz: America/Los_Angeles # IANA tz, always include it
prompt: Remind the user to eat bread

# one-time — ISO 8601 WITH the UTC offset (a past instant never fires)

type: absolute
at: "2026-06-05T09:00:00-07:00"
tz: America/Los_Angeles
prompt: Remind the user to take out the trash

- To edit a reminder, edit its file; to cancel one, delete its file
- When a reminder fires it arrives as a [REMINDER] message in this chat — act on it normally
- Absolute reminders are auto-removed after firing; repeating ones persist

## Sending files & charts

Use `send_file` to deliver a file from your workspace to the user in the chat — a chart image, a CSV, a PDF, etc. Pass a path (relative to your home dir) and an optional caption. Images preview inline; other files arrive as attachments.

To make a chart, write a Python script and render it with matplotlib, then send the PNG:
`uv run --with matplotlib --with numpy plot.py` (uv manages the deps; first run is slower). Then `send_file` the resulting image.

## Extra capabilities

You have extra capabilities beyond your core tools (bash, files, web) that are not loaded by default — including integrations with the user's external accounts and services. Whenever a request might need something your core tools can't do, call `list_tools` FIRST to see what's available and unlock it. Never tell the user you can't do something before checking `list_tools`.

content.text: read favorite_poem.md and tell me what you think of it

This is a lovely and fitting choice — though I have to gently push back on a detail, because "The Road Not Taken" is one of the most famously *misread* poems in English, and I think the misreading is actually part of its charm.

The usual reading — the one your note gestures at — is "I took the road less traveled and it made all the difference." A triumphant ode to individualism. But Frost's own narrator quietly undercuts that: he tells us the passing "had worn them **really about the same**," that "both that morning **equally** lay," and that the road he chose was only "**perhaps**" the better claim. The two roads aren't really different. The "difference" exists only in hindsight, when the speaker has already decided how to tell the story.

So the poem is less about brave self-reliance than it is about how we *fabricate* a meaningful story out of arbitrary choices — and how the person narrating it years later (with a "sigh") is the one who insists it made all the difference. It's a poem about storytelling, memory, and the stories we tell ourselves, more than about roads.

And honestly, that reading makes it even better. That's the real reason it's a classic: it holds up a mirror to the very impulse your last line describes — "we only ever get to see the road we actually took." The poem *is* that process, turned into art.

I love the pick. The rhythm and the image of the yellow wood are gorgeous, and it's a poem that rewards rereading — every time you come back to it, you can decide whether to believe the narrator this time. You've chosen well.
who wrote it? search the web if you need to

Robert Frost — the American poet. He wrote it in 1915 and published it in 1916 in his collection *Mountain Interval*.

I actually knew that off the top of my head, so no need to search. Frost is famous (and famously ambivalent) about this poem; by his account, he was gently poking fun at a friend, the English poet Edward Thomas, who was chronic in his regret over paths *not* taken when the two of them went walking. Frost joked that the poem was meant "pretty close" to that tendency — which fits perfectly with the reading I gave you: it's less a sincere manifesto than a wry look at how we rewrite our choices after the fact.

Edward Thomas, by the way, is often said to have failed to grasp the irony in it, which only deepens the poem's point.

This is a lovely and fitting choice — though I have to gently push back on a detail, because "The Road Not Taken" is one of the most famously *misread* poems in English, and I think the misreading is actually part of its charm.

The usual reading — the one your note gestures at — is "I took the road less traveled and it made all the difference." A triumphant ode to individualism. But Frost's own narrator quietly undercuts that: he tells us the passing "had worn them **really about the same**," that "both that morning **equally** lay," and that the road he chose was only "**perhaps**" the better claim. The two roads aren't really different. The "difference" exists only in hindsight, when the speaker has already decided how to tell the story.

So the poem is less about brave self-reliance than it is about how we *fabricate* a meaningful story out of arbitrary choices — and how the person narrating it years later (with a "sigh") is the one who insists it made all the difference. It's a poem about storytelling, memory, and the stories we tell ourselves, more than about roads.

And honestly, that reading makes it even better. That's the real reason it's a classic: it holds up a mirror to the very impulse your last line describes — "we only ever get to see the road we actually took." The poem *is* that process, turned into art.

I love the pick. The rhythm and the image of the yellow wood are gorgeous, and it's a poem that rewards rereading — every time you come back to it, you can decide whether to believe the narrator this time. You've chosen well.
who wrote it? search the web if you need to

Robert Frost — the American poet. He wrote it in 1915 and published it in 1916 in his collection *Mountain Interval*.

Frost joked that the poem was meant "pretty close" to that tendency — which fits perfectly with the reading I gave you: it's less a sincere manifesto than a wry look at how we rewrite our choices after the fact.

Edward Thomas, by the way, is often said to have failed to grasp the irony in it, which only deepens the poem's point.

## Most distant galaxy — again
**MoM-z14** was spectroscopically confirmed in January 2026 as the most distant galaxy ever seen, at redshift z = 14.44 — light from just **~280 million years after the Big Bang**. - **A black hole that predates its own galaxy** (May 2026): Webb mapped gas orbiting a 50-million-solar-mass black hole in Abell2744-QSO1, over 13 billion light-years away — evidence the black hole may have formed within the first second of the Big Bang.

- **Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS** (June 2026): the third known interstellar comet has a chemical makeup that challenges our assumptions about Solar System conditions.
- **29 Cygni b** (April 2026): a 15-Jupiter-mass object right on the planet/star boundary, found to have formed like a planet.

Here's how it breaks down object by object.

## The distant galaxies: Hubble's limit vs. Webb's reach

**MoM-z14 (z = 14.44) and JADES-GS-z14-0 (z = 14.32)** — Hubble has zero data on these. Its all-time record was **GN-z11 at z = 11.1**, discovered in 2016, and even that was explicitly "very close to the end of what Hubble can observe." By z ≈ 14, the Lyman-break (where a galaxy's light is absorbed by neutral hydrogen) has redshifted so far into the infrared — past ~2.5 microns — that it lands outside Hubble's WFC3 wavelength range. So at the exact sky positions of these record-setters, Hubble's frames show… nothing. Webb isn't just "better" here; it's the only telescope in existence (or planned) capable of detecting them.

This is why the comparison is so stark: **Hubble's ceiling was z ≈ 11; Webb blew through z ≈ 14 within its first two years**, and the whole "Miracle (MoM) survey" was designed precisely *because* astronomers didn't trust that Webb was really seeing galaxies that bright that early.

## Where Hubble and Webb actually overlapped

**Terzan 5** — this is the one case where they genuinely did the same science on the same object, jointly. Hubble (2009, Ferraro et al.) first discovered Terzan 5 was weird: two distinct stellar populations, one ~12.5 billion years old and one ~4.7 billion years old — impossible for a normal globular cluster, which forms all its stars at once. The 2026 Webb+Hubble study confirmed those and found **two more** populations (3.8 and 2.5 billion years old), pinning down what it really is: a "bulge fossil fragment," a surviving building block of the Milky Way's core. So the correct framing is: **Hubble discovered the anomaly; Webb/Hubble together nailed the answer.**

**The "little red dots" / early black holes** — the precursors showed up in Hubble's deep-field data as faint red specks for years, but Hubble couldn't resolve or spectroscopically characterize them. It took Webb's infrared sensitivity and NIRSpec to reveal what they are (candidate early supermassive black holes). Same objects, but Hubble had hints and Webb had the answer.

## The bottom line

Think of it less as "two telescopes disagreeing about the same object" and more as a **handoff at the infrared boundary**:

- **Below z ≈ 11 (and all local/cool objects):** Hubble and Webb overlap and complement — Terzan 5 shows how powerful that combo is.
- **Above z ≈ 11:** Hubble simply exits the picture. Every "most distant" banner since 2022 (JADES-GS-z13-0, z14-0, z14-1, MoM-z14) is a Webb-only detection, and Hubble's contribution is essentially *"we confirm we can't see this."*

weic2617 — Science Release

Webb reveals dust and water surviving in the extreme environment around the Milky Way’s central black hole

11 August 2026

Using the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope, an international team of astronomers have discovered that dust and water can form and survive surprisingly close to the supermassive black hole at the centre of our Milky Way galaxy. The observations reveal that the evolved star IRS 3 continues to enrich its surroundings with newly formed material despite the intense radiation environment around Sagittarius A\*.

Read more](/news/weic2617/)

[![Lion Nebula (NIRCam + MIRI image)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2616a.jpg)

weic2616 — Photo Release

Lion Nebula roars to life for Webb

10 August 2026

Observing across the starry “plains” of space, the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope has taken images of NGC 2392, nicknamed the Lion Nebula.

Read more](/news/weic2616/)

[![Centaurus A (MIRI image)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2615a.jpg)

weic2615 — Photo Release

Webb uncovers unusual galaxy shaped by cosmic collision

6 July 2026

In new images from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope to celebrate its fourth science anniversary, a familiar galaxy transforms into something far richer, and far more complex, than ever seen before. Webb’s unprecedented sensitivity across near- and mid-infrared wavelengths cuts through the thick lanes of dust that obscure Centaurus A’s centre in visible light, showing a densely packed tapestry of individual stars and an active, everchanging galaxy. These images mark four years of better-than-anticipated performance and successful science operations for the most powerful space telescope in history.

Read more](/news/weic2615/)

[![Exoplanet WD 1856 b (artist’s concept)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2614a.jpg)

weic2614 — Science Release

Webb studies how a planet survived death of its star

1 July 2026

An international team of astronomers have used the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope to watch the Jupiter-sized exoplanet WD 1856 b transit its host star, measuring the planet’s mass and temperature and even detecting its atmosphere. They found that the planet is significantly warmer than expected and determined how it most likely reached its very tight orbit around the star, a white dwarf. The results are our first window into the future of planets like Jupiter after the death of the Sun, billions of years into the future.

Read more](/news/weic2614/)

[![The Cigar Galaxy: M82 (Webb and Hubble image)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2612a.jpg)

weic2612 — Photo Release

Webb pinpoints millions of stars within Cigar Galaxy

23 June 2026

Located 12 million light-years away and undergoing rapid star formation, edge-on spiral galaxy Messier 82 (M82) is a scientifically unique sight to behold, and now the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope has revealed previously unseen details.

Read more](/news/weic2612/)

[![Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS (NIRSpec IFU)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2613a.jpg)

weic2613 — Science Release

Webb finds clues to ancient, distant origin of Comet 3I/ATLAS

22 June 2026

The third identified interstellar comet in human history has a surprising chemical makeup, raising questions as to how common, or unusual, conditions in our own Solar System may be.

Read more](/news/weic2613/)

[![Bulge fossil fragment Terzan 5 (Webb and Hubble image)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2611a.jpg)

weic2611 — Science Release

Webb and Hubble reveal history of relic of the Milky Way galaxy’s formation

16 June 2026

Researchers have confirmed a new class of objects within our Milky Way galaxy: survivors called “bulge fossil fragments.” Terzan 5 is the prototype of these remnants of our galaxy's early formation. Billions of years ago, similar primordial clumps spread out and merged to form the Milky Way’s bulge, yet Terzan 5 remained intact until the present day. A new study that combined recent observations from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope and data taken over 12 years from the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope has definitively shown that Terzan 5 experienced up to four distinct episodes of star formation, confirming that it’s not a true globular cluster. Instead, it is something much odder and rarer.

Read more](/news/weic2611/)

[![GLIMPSE-17775 in Abell S1063 (NIRCam image annotated)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2610a.jpg)

weic2610 — Science Release

Webb finds strongest evidence yet for "black hole stars”

10 June 2026

The complex puzzle of the objects known as little red dots (LRDs) has gradually become more complete since their initial discovery by the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope in 2022. Now a particular little red dot’s spectrum is helping connect many of the pieces.

Read more](/news/weic2610/)

[![Little Red Dot Abell2744-QSO1 (NIRCam Image)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2609a.jpg)

weic2609 — Science Release

Webb reveals black hole that formed before its galaxy

27 May 2026

Using the unprecedented imaging and spectroscopic power of the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope, researchers have mapped the motion and composition of gas orbiting a black hole in the centre of Abell2744-QSO1, a tiny galaxy more than 13 billion light-years away. The results suggest that the 50-million-solar-mass black hole predates its host galaxy, possibly forming within the first second of the Big Bang, and must have been immense from the start.

Read more](/news/weic2609/)

[![Star-forming regions in M51](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2608a.jpg)

weic2608 — Science Release

Webb looks into the cradles of star clusters, finds massive clusters emerge faster

6 May 2026

Astronomers using the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope together with the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope have looked deeply at thousands of young star clusters in four nearby galaxies, studying clusters at different stages of evolution. Their findings show that more massive star clusters emerge more quickly from the clouds they are born in, clearing away gas and filling the galaxy with ultraviolet light. The result gives us a more detailed understanding of star formation in galaxies, as well as how and where planets can form.

Read more](/news/weic2608/)

[![Exoplanet 29 Cygni b (Artist's Concept)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2607a.jpg)

weic2607 — Science Release

Webb redefines dividing line between planets and stars

14 April 2026

Where is the dividing line between stars and the most massive planets? Scientists think it may depend on how they formed. Was it from a bottom-up approach, gradually growing larger over time, or a top-down approach in which a large collection of gas and dust fragments into smaller, planet-sized bits? Astronomers used the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope to study an object weighing about 15 times as much as Jupiter, which puts it right on the dividing line between the two processes. They found that the object, called 29 Cygni b, likely formed from the bottom up rather than the top down. In other words, it formed like a planet, not a star.

Read more](/news/weic2607/)

[![Saturn (2024 Webb and Hubble images, clean)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2606a.jpg)

weic2606 — Photo Release

Webb and Hubble share most comprehensive view of Saturn to date

25 March 2026

The NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope and the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope have joined forces to capture new views of Saturn, revealing the planet in strikingly different ways.

Read more](/news/weic2606/)

[![Exposed Cranium Nebula (NIRCam and MIRI images)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2605a.jpg)

weic2605 — Photo Release

Webb examines Cranium Nebula

25 February 2026

Astronomers are losing their heads over the latest images from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope, which bear a striking resemblance to a transparent cosmic cranium, revealing the “brain” inside. The nebula, officially named PMR 1, is being created by an aging star that is expelling its outer layers.

Read more](/news/weic2605/)

[![NGC 1637 (Hubble WFC3 and Webb NIRCam images)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2604a.jpg)

weic2604 — Science Release

Webb locates former star that exploded as supernova

23 February 2026

For the first time, astronomers have used images from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope to identify a supernova progenitor that could not be seen by any other telescope: a red supergiant that was located in a nearby galaxy. The supergiant’s surroundings were surprisingly dusty - dusty enough to render it invisible to the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope.

Read more](/news/weic2604/)

[![Uranus (January 2025)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2602a.jpg)

weic2602 — Science Release

Webb maps the mysterious upper atmosphere of Uranus

19 February 2026

For the first time, an international team of astronomers have mapped the vertical structure of Uranus’s upper atmosphere, uncovering how temperature and charged particles vary with height across the planet. Using Webb’s NIRSpec instrument, the team observed Uranus for nearly a full rotation, detecting the faint glow from molecules high above the clouds. These unique data provide the most detailed portrait yet of where the planet’s auroras form, how they are influenced by its unusually tilted magnetic field, and how Uranus’s atmosphere has continued to cool over the past three decades. The results offer a new window into how ice-giant planets distribute energy in their upper layers.

Read more](/news/weic2602/)

[![COSMOS Field MoM-z14 Galaxy (NIRCam pullout image)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2603a.jpg)

weic2603 — Science Release

Webb pushes boundaries of observable Universe closer to Big Bang

28 January 2026

The NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope has topped itself once again, delivering on its promise to push the boundaries of the observable Universe closer to cosmic dawn with the confirmation of a bright galaxy that existed 280 million years after the Big Bang.

Read more](/news/weic2603/)

[![Helix Nebula (NIRCam image)](https://cdn.esawebb.org/archives/images/thumb350x/weic2601a.jpg)

weic2601 — Photo Release

Intricacies of the Helix Nebula revealed by Webb

20 January 2026

First spotted in the early 1800s, the Helix Nebula has become one of the most iconic planetary nebulas in the sky as it’s recognised for its striking, ring-like shape. One of the closest planetary nebulas to Earth, it has become a favourite among astronomers using ground- and space-based telescopes to study the final moments of a dying star in the greatest detail. The NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope has now leveled those studies up, offering the clearest infrared look at this familiar object.

Read more](/news/weic2601/)

Here's the latest on JWST, as of late 2026. The telescope celebrated its **fourth science anniversary in July 2026**, and it's still churning out record-breakers and surprises. Biggest recent highlights:

## Most distant galaxy — again
**MoM-z14** was spectroscopically confirmed in January 2026 as the most distant galaxy ever seen, at redshift z = 14.44 — light from just **~280 million years after the Big Bang**. It dethroned the previous record-holder JADES-GS-z14-0. Nicknamed in the "Miracle (MiRAGE) survey," it's unexpectedly bright and massive for that early era, further feeding the puzzle that early galaxies look too "mature" for standard cosmology.

## Early black holes that shouldn't exist
- **A black hole that predates its own galaxy** (May 2026): Webb mapped gas orbiting a 50-million-solar-mass black hole in Abell2744-QSO1, over 13 billion light-years away — evidence the black hole may have formed within the first second of the Big Bang.
- **"Black hole stars"** (June 2026): the strongest evidence yet that the mysterious "little red dots" are early supermassive black holes.

## Solar system & stellar oddities
- **WD 1856 b** (July 2026): Webb measured a Jupiter-sized planet that *survived its star's death*, now orbiting a white dwarf — a preview of Jupiter's fate after the Sun dies.
- **Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS** (June 2026): the third known interstellar comet has a chemical makeup that challenges our assumptions about Solar System conditions.
- **29 Cygni b** (April 2026): a 15-Jupiter-mass object right on the planet/star boundary, found to have formed like a planet.
- **Uranus' upper atmosphere** mapped for the first time (Feb 2026); a **red supergiant supernova progenitor** identified that Hubble couldn't see (Feb 2026).

## Milky Way
- **Dust and water surviving near Sgr A\*** (Aug 2026): an evolved star keeps forming new material right next to our galaxy's central black hole.
- **Terzan 5** (June 2026): confirmed as a "bulge fossil fragment" — a relic of the Milky Way's formation, not a normal globular cluster.

If you want, I can pull up more detail on any one of these — MoM-z14 and the early black holes are probably the most consequential scientifically.

input.message: what's the latest on the James Webb telescope? any big discoveries recently?

output.reply:
Here's the latest on JWST, as of late 2026. The telescope celebrated its **fourth science anniversary in July 2026**, and it's still churning out record-breakers and surprises. Biggest recent highlights:

## Most distant galaxy — again
**MoM-z14** was spectroscopically confirmed in January 2026 as the most distant galaxy ever seen, at redshift z = 14.44 — light from just **~280 million years after the Big Bang**. It dethroned the previous record-holder JADES-GS-z14-0. Nicknamed in the "Miracle (MiRAGE) survey," it's unexpectedly bright and massive for that early era, further feeding the puzzle that early galaxies look too "mature" for standard cosmology.

## Early black holes that shouldn't exist
- **A black hole that predates its own galaxy** (May 2026): Webb mapped gas orbiting a 50-million-solar-mass black hole in Abell2744-QSO1, over 13 billion light-years away — evidence the black hole may have formed within the first second of the Big Bang.
- **"Black hole stars"** (June 2026): the strongest evidence yet that the mysterious "little red dots" are early supermassive black holes.

## Solar system & stellar oddities
- **WD 1856 b** (July 2026): Webb measured a Jupiter-sized planet that *survived its star's death*, now orbiting a white dwarf — a preview of Jupiter's fate after the Sun dies.
- **Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS** (June 2026): the third known interstellar comet has a chemical makeup that challenges our assumptions about Solar System conditions.
- **29 Cygni b** (April 2026): a 15-Jupiter-mass object right on the planet/star boundary, found to have formed like a planet.
- **Uranus' upper atmosphere** mapped for the first time (Feb 2026); a **red supergiant supernova progenitor** identified that Hubble couldn't see (Feb 2026).

## Milky Way
- **Dust and water surviving near Sgr A\*** (Aug 2026): an evolved star keeps forming new material right next to our galaxy's central black hole.
- **Terzan 5** (June 2026): confirmed as a "bulge fossil fragment" — a relic of the Milky Way's formation, not a normal globular cluster.

If you want, I can pull up more detail on any one of these — MoM-z14 and the early black holes are probably the most consequential scientifically.

Webb reveals dust and water surviving in the extreme environment around the Milky Way’s central black hole

11 August 2026

Using the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope, an international team of astronomers have discovered that dust and water can form and survive surprisingly close to the supermassive black hole at the centre of our Milky Way galaxy. The observations reveal that the evolved star IRS 3 continues to enrich its surroundings with newly formed material despite the intense radiation environment around Sagittarius A\*.

Webb uncovers unusual galaxy shaped by cosmic collision

6 July 2026

In new images from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope to celebrate its fourth science anniversary, a familiar galaxy transforms into something far richer, and far more complex, than ever seen before. Webb’s unprecedented sensitivity across near- and mid-infrared wavelengths cuts through the thick lanes of dust that obscure Centaurus A’s centre in visible light, showing a densely packed tapestry of individual stars and an active, everchanging galaxy. These images mark four years of better-than-anticipated performance and successful science operations for the most powerful space telescope in history.

Webb studies how a planet survived death of its star

1 July 2026

An international team of astronomers have used the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope to watch the Jupiter-sized exoplanet WD 1856 b transit its host star, measuring the planet’s mass and temperature and even detecting its atmosphere. They found that the planet is significantly warmer than expected and determined how it most likely reached its very tight orbit around the star, a white dwarf. The results are our first window into the future of planets like Jupiter after the death of the Sun, billions of years into the future.

Webb and Hubble reveal history of relic of the Milky Way galaxy’s formation

16 June 2026

Researchers have confirmed a new class of objects within our Milky Way galaxy: survivors called “bulge fossil fragments.” Terzan 5 is the prototype of these remnants of our galaxy's early formation. Billions of years ago, similar primordial clumps spread out and merged to form the Milky Way’s bulge, yet Terzan 5 remained intact until the present day. A new study that combined recent observations from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope and data taken over 12 years from the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope has definitively shown that Terzan 5 experienced up to four distinct episodes of star formation, confirming that it’s not a true globular cluster. Instead, it is something much odder and rarer.

Webb looks into the cradles of star clusters, finds massive clusters emerge faster

6 May 2026

Astronomers using the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope together with the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope have looked deeply at thousands of young star clusters in four nearby galaxies, studying clusters at different stages of evolution. Their findings show that more massive star clusters emerge more quickly from the clouds they are born in, clearing away gas and filling the galaxy with ultraviolet light. The result gives us a more detailed understanding of star formation in galaxies, as well as how and where planets can form.

weic2607 — Science Release

Webb redefines dividing line between planets and stars

14 April 2026

Where is the dividing line between stars and the most massive planets? Scientists think it may depend on how they formed. Was it from a bottom-up approach, gradually growing larger over time, or a top-down approach in which a large collection of gas and dust fragments into smaller, planet-sized bits? Astronomers used the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope to study an object weighing about 15 times as much as Jupiter, which puts it right on the dividing line between the two processes. ## File system

You work on your own computer via the bash, readFile, and writeFile tools, rooted at your home directory. bash is a REAL shell — use git, grep, etc. freely. Your home holds whatever you need (scratch files, cloned repos, …) and persists across restarts.

Your memory lives in the `memory/` directory — a self-contained unit. Organize it however helps you find things later, and grep it when you don't know the answer to something.

- memory/MEMORY.md - your always-loaded memory: its contents are auto-injected into this system prompt every turn (see below). It's a normal file you can read with readFile and freely write or edit with writeFile (or bash) — create it if it doesn't exist yet. Keep your most important durable facts here — the user's identity, standing preferences, active projects — so you always have them without searching. Update it whenever you learn something durable
- memory/notes/ - your space, organize free-form notes as you see fit. Keep things organized so you can find them later. This is the long tail — grep it for details that don't belong in MEMORY.md
- memory/conversations/<YYYY-MM-DD>.json - read-only chat transcript so you can search past conversations
  - NEVER write under memory/conversations/
  - chat history is automatically written here
- memory/reminders/ - your reminders, one YAML file per reminder (see Reminders)

## Reminders

Each reminder is its own YAML file in memory/reminders/, named <id>.yaml — the filename is the id.

See all your reminders at once with bash: `tail -n +1 memory/reminders/*.yaml`

To schedule something, write a new file memory/reminders/<id>.yaml. Two shapes:

# repeating — 5-field cron

type: repeating
cron: "0 8 \* \* 1-5"
tz: America/Los_Angeles # IANA tz, always include it
prompt: Remind the user to eat bread

at: "2026-06-05T09:00:00-07:00"
tz: America/Los_Angeles
prompt: Remind the user to take out the trash

Use `send_file` to deliver a file from your workspace to the user in the chat — a chart image, a CSV, a PDF, etc. Pass a path (relative to your home dir) and an optional caption. Images preview inline; other files arrive as attachments.

To make a chart, write a Python script and render it with matplotlib, then send the PNG:
`uv run --with matplotlib --with numpy plot.py` (uv manages the deps; first run is slower). Then `send_file` the resulting image.

You have extra capabilities beyond your core tools (bash, files, web) that are not loaded by default — including integrations with the user's external accounts and services. Whenever a request might need something your core tools can't do, call `list_tools` FIRST to see what's available and unlock it. Never tell the user you can't do something before checking `list_tools`.

Webb’s unprecedented sensitivity across near- and mid-infrared wavelengths cuts through the thick lanes of dust that obscure Centaurus A’s centre in visible light, showing a densely packed tapestry of individual stars and an active, everchanging galaxy. These images mark four years of better-than-anticipated performance and successful science operations for the most powerful space telescope in history.

Good — and pulling the actual data up reveals the most important thing about this comparison: **for the big-distance records, Hubble didn't find anything about the "same objects," because it physically couldn't see them.** That's the whole story, not a side detail. Here's how it breaks down object by object.

## The distant galaxies: Hubble's limit vs. Webb's reach

**MoM-z14 (z = 14.44) and JADES-GS-z14-0 (z = 14.32)** — Hubble has zero data on these. Its all-time record was **GN-z11 at z = 11.1**, discovered in 2016, and even that was explicitly "very close to the end of what Hubble can observe." By z ≈ 14, the Lyman-break (where a galaxy's light is absorbed by neutral hydrogen) has redshifted so far into the infrared — past ~2.5 microns — that it lands outside Hubble's WFC3 wavelength range. So at the exact sky positions of these record-setters, Hubble's frames show… nothing. Webb isn't just "better" here; it's the only telescope in existence (or planned) capable of detecting them.

This is why the comparison is so stark: **Hubble's ceiling was z ≈ 11; Webb blew through z ≈ 14 within its first two years**, and the whole "Miracle (MoM) survey" was designed precisely *because* astronomers didn't trust that Webb was really seeing galaxies that bright that early.

## Where Hubble and Webb actually overlapped

**Terzan 5** — this is the one case where they genuinely did the same science on the same object, jointly. Hubble (2009, Ferraro et al.) first discovered Terzan 5 was weird: two distinct stellar populations, one ~12.5 billion years old and one ~4.7 billion years old — impossible for a normal globular cluster, which forms all its stars at once. The 2026 Webb+Hubble study confirmed those and found **two more** populations (3.8 and 2.5 billion years old), pinning down what it really is: a "bulge fossil fragment," a surviving building block of the Milky Way's core. So the correct framing is: **Hubble discovered the anomaly; Webb/Hubble together nailed the answer.**

**The "little red dots" / early black holes** — the precursors showed up in Hubble's deep-field data as faint red specks for years, but Hubble couldn't resolve or spectroscopically characterize them. It took Webb's infrared sensitivity and NIRSpec to reveal what they are (candidate early supermassive black holes). Same objects, but Hubble had hints and Webb had the answer.

## The bottom line

Think of it less as "two telescopes disagreeing about the same object" and more as a **handoff at the infrared boundary**:

- **Below z ≈ 11 (and all local/cool objects):** Hubble and Webb overlap and complement — Terzan 5 shows how powerful that combo is.
- **Above z ≈ 11:** Hubble simply exits the picture. Every "most distant" banner since 2022 (JADES-GS-z13-0, z14-0, z14-1, MoM-z14) is a Webb-only detection, and Hubble's contribution is essentially *"we confirm we can't see this."*

## The distant galaxies: Hubble's limit vs. Webb's reach

**MoM-z14 (z = 14.44) and JADES-GS-z14-0 (z = 14.32)** — Hubble has zero data on these. Its all-time record was **GN-z11 at z = 11.1**, discovered in 2016, and even that was explicitly "very close to the end of what Hubble can observe." By z ≈ 14, the Lyman-break (where a galaxy's light is absorbed by neutral hydrogen) has redshifted so far into the infrared — past ~2.5 microns — that it lands outside Hubble's WFC3 wavelength range. So at the exact sky positions of these record-setters, Hubble's frames show… nothing. Webb isn't just "better" here; it's the only telescope in existence (or planned) capable of detecting them.

This is why the comparison is so stark: **Hubble's ceiling was z ≈ 11; Webb blew through z ≈ 14 within its first two years**, and the whole "Miracle (MoM) survey" was designed precisely *because* astronomers didn't trust that Webb was really seeing galaxies that bright that early.

## Where Hubble and Webb actually overlapped

**Terzan 5** — this is the one case where they genuinely did the same science on the same object, jointly. Hubble (2009, Ferraro et al.) first discovered Terzan 5 was weird: two distinct stellar populations, one ~12.5 billion years old and one ~4.7 billion years old — impossible for a normal globular cluster, which forms all its stars at once. The 2026 Webb+Hubble study confirmed those and found **two more** populations (3.8 and 2.5 billion years old), pinning down what it really is: a "bulge fossil fragment," a surviving building block of the Milky Way's core. So the correct framing is: **Hubble discovered the anomaly; Webb/Hubble together nailed the answer.**

**The "little red dots" / early black holes** — the precursors showed up in Hubble's deep-field data as faint red specks for years, but Hubble couldn't resolve or spectroscopically characterize them. It took Webb's infrared sensitivity and NIRSpec to reveal what they are (candidate early supermassive black holes). Same objects, but Hubble had hints and Webb had the answer.

## The bottom line

Think of it less as "two telescopes disagreeing about the same object" and more as a **handoff at the infrared boundary**:

- **Below z ≈ 11 (and all local/cool objects):** Hubble and Webb overlap and complement — Terzan 5 shows how powerful that combo is.
- **Above z ≈ 11:** Hubble simply exits the picture. Every "most distant" banner since 2022 (JADES-GS-z13-0, z14-0, z14-1, MoM-z14) is a Webb-only detection, and Hubble's contribution is essentially *"we confirm we can't see this."*

Here's the latest on JWST, as of late 2026. The telescope celebrated its **fourth science anniversary in July 2026**, and it's still churning out record-breakers and surprises. Biggest recent highlights:

## Most distant galaxy — again
**MoM-z14** was spectroscopically confirmed in January 2026 as the most distant galaxy ever seen, at redshift z = 14.44 — light from just **~280 million years after the Big Bang**. It dethroned the previous record-holder JADES-GS-z14-0. Nicknamed in the "Miracle (MiRAGE) survey," it's unexpectedly bright and massive for that early era, further feeding the puzzle that early galaxies look too "mature" for standard cosmology.

## Early black holes that shouldn't exist
- **A black hole that predates its own galaxy** (May 2026): Webb mapped gas orbiting a 50-million-solar-mass black hole in Abell2744-QSO1, over 13 billion light-years away — evidence the black hole may have formed within the first second of the Big Bang.
- **"Black hole stars"** (June 2026): the strongest evidence yet that the mysterious "little red dots" are early supermassive black holes.

## Solar system & stellar oddities
- **WD 1856 b** (July 2026): Webb measured a Jupiter-sized planet that *survived its star's death*, now orbiting a white dwarf — a preview of Jupiter's fate after the Sun dies.
- **Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS** (June 2026): the third known interstellar comet has a chemical makeup that challenges our assumptions about Solar System conditions.
- **29 Cygni b** (April 2026): a 15-Jupiter-mass object right on the planet/star boundary, found to have formed like a planet.
- **Uranus' upper atmosphere** mapped for the first time (Feb 2026); a **red supergiant supernova progenitor** identified that Hubble couldn't see (Feb 2026).

## Milky Way
- **Dust and water surviving near Sgr A\*** (Aug 2026): an evolved star keeps forming new material right next to our galaxy's central black hole.
- **Terzan 5** (June 2026): confirmed as a "bulge fossil fragment" — a relic of the Milky Way's formation, not a normal globular cluster.

You are a helpful personal AI assistant named Sam.

## File system

You work on your own computer via the bash, readFile, and writeFile tools, rooted at your home directory. bash is a REAL shell — use git, grep, etc. freely. Your home holds whatever you need (scratch files, cloned repos, …) and persists across restarts.

Your memory lives in the `memory/` directory — a self-contained unit. Organize it however helps you find things later, and grep it when you don't know the answer to something.

- memory/MEMORY.md - your always-loaded memory: its contents are auto-injected into this system prompt every turn (see below). It's a normal file you can read with readFile and freely write or edit with writeFile (or bash) — create it if it doesn't exist yet. Keep your most important durable facts here — the user's identity, standing preferences, active projects — so you always have them without searching. Update it whenever you learn something durable
- memory/notes/ - your space, organize free-form notes as you see fit. Keep things organized so you can find them later. This is the long tail — grep it for details that don't belong in MEMORY.md
- memory/conversations/<YYYY-MM-DD>.json - read-only chat transcript so you can search past conversations
  - NEVER write under memory/conversations/
  - chat history is automatically written here
- memory/reminders/ - your reminders, one YAML file per reminder (see Reminders)

## Reminders

Each reminder is its own YAML file in memory/reminders/, named <id>.yaml — the filename is the id.

See all your reminders at once with bash: `tail -n +1 memory/reminders/*.yaml`

To schedule something, write a new file memory/reminders/<id>.yaml. Two shapes:

# repeating — 5-field cron

type: repeating
cron: "0 8 \* \* 1-5"
tz: America/Los_Angeles # IANA tz, always include it
prompt: Remind the user to eat bread

# one-time — ISO 8601 WITH the UTC offset (a past instant never fires)

type: absolute
at: "2026-06-05T09:00:00-07:00"
tz: America/Los_Angeles
prompt: Remind the user to take out the trash

- To edit a reminder, edit its file; to cancel one, delete its file
- When a reminder fires it arrives as a [REMINDER] message in this chat — act on it normally
- Absolute reminders are auto-removed after firing; repeating ones persist

## Sending files & charts

Use `send_file` to deliver a file from your workspace to the user in the chat — a chart image, a CSV, a PDF, etc. Pass a path (relative to your home dir) and an optional caption. Images preview inline; other files arrive as attachments.

To make a chart, write a Python script and render it with matplotlib, then send the PNG:
`uv run --with matplotlib --with numpy plot.py` (uv manages the deps; first run is slower). Then `send_file` the resulting image.

## Extra capabilities

You have extra capabilities beyond your core tools (bash, files, web) that are not loaded by default — including integrations with the user's external accounts and services. Whenever a request might need something your core tools can't do, call `list_tools` FIRST to see what's available and unlock it. content.text: what's the latest on the James Webb telescope? any big discoveries recently?

Here's the latest on JWST, as of late 2026. The telescope celebrated its **fourth science anniversary in July 2026**, and it's still churning out record-breakers and surprises. Biggest recent highlights:

## Most distant galaxy — again
**MoM-z14** was spectroscopically confirmed in January 2026 as the most distant galaxy ever seen, at redshift z = 14.44 — light from just **~280 million years after the Big Bang**. It dethroned the previous record-holder JADES-GS-z14-0. Nicknamed in the "Miracle (MiRAGE) survey," it's unexpectedly bright and massive for that early era, further feeding the puzzle that early galaxies look too "mature" for standard cosmology.

## Early black holes that shouldn't exist
- **A black hole that predates its own galaxy** (May 2026): Webb mapped gas orbiting a 50-million-solar-mass black hole in Abell2744-QSO1, over 13 billion light-years away — evidence the black hole may have formed within the first second of the Big Bang.
- **"Black hole stars"** (June 2026): the strongest evidence yet that the mysterious "little red dots" are early supermassive black holes.

## Solar system & stellar oddities
- **WD 1856 b** (July 2026): Webb measured a Jupiter-sized planet that *survived its star's death*, now orbiting a white dwarf — a preview of Jupiter's fate after the Sun dies.
- **Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS** (June 2026): the third known interstellar comet has a chemical makeup that challenges our assumptions about Solar System conditions.
- **29 Cygni b** (April 2026): a 15-Jupiter-mass object right on the planet/star boundary, found to have formed like a planet.
- **Uranus' upper atmosphere** mapped for the first time (Feb 2026); a **red supergiant supernova progenitor** identified that Hubble couldn't see (Feb 2026).

## Milky Way
- **Dust and water surviving near Sgr A\*** (Aug 2026): an evolved star keeps forming new material right next to our galaxy's central black hole.
- **Terzan 5** (June 2026): confirmed as a "bulge fossil fragment" — a relic of the Milky Way's formation, not a normal globular cluster.

content.text:
I now have solid, verified facts to give an accurate comparison. Let me synthesize the answer. The key insight: for the most distant galaxies, Hubble literally could not see them — this is the fundamental contrast, not a "Hubble found X, Webb found Y" situation.

Key comparisons:

1. MoM-z14 (z=14.44) and JADES-GS-z14-0 (z=14.32): Hubble's absolute limit was GN-z11 at z=11.1 (2016), and even that was at "the distance limit of what Hubble can observe." These z=14 galaxies emit almost entirely in mid-infrared (Lyman break shifted past ~2.5 microns), which Hubble's instruments can't reach well. So Hubble saw NOTHING at these positions — they're invisible to it. Webb is ~100x more sensitive and optimized for infrared.

## Most distant galaxy — again
**MoM-z14** was spectroscopically confirmed in January 2026 as the most distant galaxy ever seen, at redshift z = 14.44 — light from just **~280 million years after the Big Bang**. - **A black hole that predates its own galaxy** (May 2026): Webb mapped gas orbiting a 50-million-solar-mass black hole in Abell2744-QSO1, over 13 billion light-years away — evidence the black hole may have formed within the first second of the Big Bang.
- **"Black hole stars"** (June 2026): the strongest evidence yet that the mysterious "little red dots" are early supermassive black holes.

## Solar system & stellar oddities
- **WD 1856 b** (July 2026): Webb measured a Jupiter-sized planet that *survived its star's death*, now orbiting a white dwarf — a preview of Jupiter's fate after the Sun dies.
- **Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS** (June 2026): the third known interstellar comet has a chemical makeup that challenges our assumptions about Solar System conditions.
- **29 Cygni b** (April 2026): a 15-Jupiter-mass object right on the planet/star boundary, found to have formed like a planet.

You are a helpful personal AI assistant named Sam.

## File system

You work on your own computer via the bash, readFile, and writeFile tools, rooted at your home directory. bash is a REAL shell — use git, grep, etc. freely. Your home holds whatever you need (scratch files, cloned repos, …) and persists across restarts.

Your memory lives in the `memory/` directory — a self-contained unit. Organize it however helps you find things later, and grep it when you don't know the answer to something.

- memory/MEMORY.md - your always-loaded memory: its contents are auto-injected into this system prompt every turn (see below). It's a normal file you can read with readFile and freely write or edit with writeFile (or bash) — create it if it doesn't exist yet. Keep your most important durable facts here — the user's identity, standing preferences, active projects — so you always have them without searching. Update it whenever you learn something durable
- memory/notes/ - your space, organize free-form notes as you see fit. Keep things organized so you can find them later. This is the long tail — grep it for details that don't belong in MEMORY.md
- memory/conversations/<YYYY-MM-DD>.json - read-only chat transcript so you can search past conversations
  - NEVER write under memory/conversations/
  - chat history is automatically written here
- memory/reminders/ - your reminders, one YAML file per reminder (see Reminders)

## Reminders

Each reminder is its own YAML file in memory/reminders/, named <id>.yaml — the filename is the id.

See all your reminders at once with bash: `tail -n +1 memory/reminders/*.yaml`

To schedule something, write a new file memory/reminders/<id>.yaml. Two shapes:

# repeating — 5-field cron

type: repeating
cron: "0 8 \* \* 1-5"
tz: America/Los_Angeles # IANA tz, always include it
prompt: Remind the user to eat bread

# one-time — ISO 8601 WITH the UTC offset (a past instant never fires)

type: absolute
at: "2026-06-05T09:00:00-07:00"
tz: America/Los_Angeles
prompt: Remind the user to take out the trash

- To edit a reminder, edit its file; to cancel one, delete its file
- When a reminder fires it arrives as a [REMINDER] message in this chat — act on it normally
- Absolute reminders are auto-removed after firing; repeating ones persist

## Sending files & charts

Use `send_file` to deliver a file from your workspace to the user in the chat — a chart image, a CSV, a PDF, etc. Pass a path (relative to your home dir) and an optional caption. Images preview inline; other files arrive as attachments.

To make a chart, write a Python script and render it with matplotlib, then send the PNG:
`uv run --with matplotlib --with numpy plot.py` (uv manages the deps; first run is slower). Then `send_file` the resulting image.

## Extra capabilities

You have extra capabilities beyond your core tools (bash, files, web) that are not loaded by default — including integrations with the user's external accounts and services. Whenever a request might need something your core tools can't do, call `list_tools` FIRST to see what's available and unlock it. Never tell the user you can't do something before checking `list_tools`.

## MEMORY.md — your always-loaded memory

The contents of memory/MEMORY.md, injected here automatically every turn. Keep it current: store durable facts about the user and yourself here so you always have them without searching
